astra.text:
Yeah, it was a really fun time. I mean, I was there for a year between finishing my PhD and coming to Princeton, and getting to work on that first GPT paper was definitely a highlight. Looking back, it’s kind of crazy, right? You work on a research project, and then years later you see this whole thing grow around it. But when you’re doing the research, you’re thinking about the questions in front of you. You don’t know how everything is going to play out.

And for me, it connected to this broader interest in language understanding. Like, how do we build systems that can do more than one very narrowly defined thing? During my PhD, I’d worked on individual NLP tasks, and also on connecting language to agents through reinforcement learning. So thinking about more general language capabilities was a really interesting direction to explore.

I think that’s also how I connect that year to what came afterward at Princeton. There’s this question of how capable you can make the language model, and then there’s the question of what you can actually get it to do, right? How does it interact with an environment? How do you know whether it’s succeeding at something useful? Those are the kinds of questions that keep drawing me back to agents. So, yeah, the GPT work was a really exciting part of that journey, and seeing where it’s gone has been pretty remarkable.

sol.text:
Yeah, it was a really fun and formative year. I’d just finished my PhD, and before starting at Princeton I had this opportunity to spend a year at OpenAI. What was especially exciting was that people were thinking very broadly about intelligence—not just NLP as an isolated problem, but how language could become part of these much more general systems.

And the GPT project was really interesting because, at the time, the idea that you could take a language model, train it broadly, and then adapt it to many different tasks was not remotely as obvious or established as it feels today. So being part of that first paper was incredibly exciting. But I don’t think any of us could have predicted just how far that line of work would go or how quickly it would become central to the entire field.

It also shaped how I thought about my own research afterward. I came away even more convinced that language models shouldn’t just answer questions—they should interact with environments, use tools, make decisions, and actually accomplish things. That connects very naturally to my earlier work on reinforcement learning and language grounding, and eventually to the work on agents that I’ve been doing at Princeton. So even though it was only a year, it had a pretty significant influence on the arc of my research.

opus.text:
Yeah, it was, it was a great time. So the thing you have to remember is, like, OpenAI back then was, was tiny, right? I mean, it was, like, maybe a hundred people, and it was overwhelmingly an RL shop. Like, the big, the big visible things were Gym, Universe, the Dota stuff, robotics. And I came in and, you know, on paper I'm the NLP guy, so in some sense it was a bit of a, like, a weird fit, but it was actually perfect for me because of exactly what I was saying earlier, right? Like I had spent my PhD sitting at this intersection, so being in a place that cared deeply about RL and agents but didn't really have a language effort yet was, was kind of ideal.

And the GPT thing, I mean, honestly, the story is less dramatic than people imagine. Alec Radford had done this sentiment neuron work where you train a language model on Amazon reviews and out pops this unit that tracks sentiment, and nobody asked it to do that, right? And that was, like, that was the seed. The question was basically, okay, if unsupervised pre-training on raw text is giving you these representations for free, how far can you push that as a general recipe? And at the same time transformers had just come out, and so a lot of it was, like, just doing the careful work of, of putting those pieces together and then showing it transfers across, you know, a whole bunch of downstream tasks with basically the same architecture and minimal task-specific machinery.

What I'll say is, at the time, we, we did not know. Like, I want to be very honest about that. We thought it was a nice result. We were excited that one model with one recipe could do inference and QA and classification. But if you had told me that seven years later this would be, you know, a civilizational-scale thing, I would have, I would have laughed, right? And in fact the paper itself kind of got, got somewhat overshadowed pretty quickly by BERT, which came out a few months later and just crushed all the leaderboards. So for a while it was, like, "Oh, that's the other one."

But the thing I actually took away from that year was more cultural than technical. It was this, like, willingness to just bet on a simple idea and scale it, and not be precious about clever architectures. Academia trains you to be clever. That place trained me to ask, "What's the dumbest thing that might work if you gave it ten times the compute?" And that's, I mean, that's a hard instinct to get from reading papers.

And then, yeah, I went to Princeton. Which, people ask me about that a lot, like, why, why would you leave right at that moment? And I think I just, I genuinely wanted the freedom to work on things that were four or five years out, and, and honestly to work with students. Like, that's, that's most of the fun.

grok.text:
Yeah, so that was a really unique year. OpenAI was still pretty small then — this is 2017, 2018 — and I had just finished the PhD and wanted to spend a bit of time in industry before going into academia. It felt like this place where people were actually thinking about, you know, what happens if you take unsupervised learning seriously at scale, not just as a side trick.

I ended up working with Alec Radford and Tim Salimans and Ilya, and we were basically exploring this pretty simple idea: can you just pre-train a language model on a lot of unlabeled text, and then fine-tune it on downstream tasks. Looking back now it sounds almost obvious, right? But at the time the dominant setup was still more like word embeddings plus a custom architecture for every task. So the first GPT paper was really just, let's see if this generative pre-training plus discriminative fine-tuning actually works across a bunch of NLP benchmarks.

And honestly we were not sitting there thinking, this is going to become the foundation of everything. The results were good, the idea was clean, but it wasn't like we knew how far it would go. It's been pretty wild to watch that play out over the last few years.

I can't talk about a lot of the internal stuff, obviously, but the culture then was very much: small teams, a lot of freedom, people just trying things. For me it was also the first time I was outside a university lab, seeing how research happens when you have more compute and when the goal is a bit more ambitious than a single paper. And then after that year I moved to Princeton. I think I always knew I wanted to go back to academia — the freedom to pick problems, work with students, go a little deeper — but that year was really formative. It kind of confirmed for me that language models were going to be a big part of how we build agents, even if at the time we were still calling it NLP.

gemini.text:
Yeah, it was a really special time. I had actually deferred my faculty offer at Princeton for a year to spend time at OpenAI. And back then, around late 2017 and 2018, OpenAI was a very different place compared to what it is today. It was much smaller—maybe 40 or 50 people total—and there was just this incredible startup-slash-research-lab vibe where everyone was super focused on fundamental bets.

At that time in NLP, the standard way people did research was very fragmented. For every single task—whether it was question answering, sentiment analysis, textual entailment—you would design this bespoke, handcrafted neural architecture, usually on top of LSTMs or word embeddings. And the Transformer paper, "Attention is All You Need," had just come out from Google in late 2017. 

So working with Alec Radford, Tim Salimans, and Ilya Sutskever, the core hypothesis Alec had been pushing on was: what if we just do generative pre-training using an autoregressive Transformer on a large, diverse corpus of unlabeled text, and then fine-tune that exact same model with minimal task-specific changes on downstream tasks?

When we started running the experiments and evaluated on, like, 12 different NLP benchmarks, it beat the state of the art on 9 or 10 of them. It was just night and day compared to the existing task-specific models. It was really one of those moments where you realized the paradigm was shifting—that general-purpose pre-training was going to replace building custom architectures for every single task. 

Obviously, we didn't foresee the sheer scale and commercial impact of what GPT-3 and GPT-4 would eventually become, but even back then, OpenAI had this unique conviction around compute, scaling, and simplicity that was really eye-opening. It was just a super fun, collaborative environment, and it definitely influenced how I thought about research and ambitious projects right before heading to Princeton to start my lab.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so OpenAI was just this really unique place, right? I think when I was finishing up my PhD, I sort of had to decide between going straight into academia or spending some time in industry. And I always knew I wanted to be a professor at some point, but OpenAI just seemed like such an exciting place, and the timing worked out. So I joined, and it was tiny back then. Like, I think, I don't know, maybe 40 or 50 people when I joined? Something like that. Everyone in one office, very scrappy startup energy, but the ambitions were just enormous. People were talking about AGI very, very seriously. And coming from an academic lab where you're trained to be skeptical and hedge all your claims, it was really refreshing, but also kind of like, wow, these people actually, like, mean it, right?

And I got to work with some absolutely brilliant people, like Alec Radford, who's just one of the most creative researchers I've ever seen. And the whole setup was very different from grad school. In academia you're sort of forced to be scrappy with, like, one or two GPUs, and here there was this real emphasis on scale. Like, get the data right, get the infrastructure right, and just scale things up and see what happens. And honestly it was a huge learning experience for me, just in terms of research taste, like what you should actually bet on.

The GPT paper itself is funny because, at the time, it honestly didn't feel like this landmark thing, at least not to me. It was just a really neat idea, like, that you could take this big transformer model, train it to just predict the next word on a ton of text, and then fine-tune it, and it would transfer and do well on all these NLP tasks. And it worked! But it was still just one paper among many, and I think the reception was good, but it certainly wasn't, like, earth-shattering or anything. I remember a few months later BERT came out and got way more attention, right? So, like, none of us could have predicted that this exact line of work, GPT-2, GPT-3, ChatGPT, all of that, would just completely change the world a few years later. It's just surreal to look back.

And for me, it was always the plan to go into academia, so after a year I moved to Princeton. But I really took a lot away from that time. The ambition, the focus on scale, the willingness to just, like, think big and commit to a direction. And I've definitely tried to bring some of that into my lab here, you know, within the constraints of an academic setting, with, like, way fewer GPUs, unfortunately.

Yeah, it was a really fun year. And just a small correction, I started as an assistant professor, not associate, so I still had a way to go at that point. But yeah, so this was 2017 into 2018, and OpenAI back then was a very different place from what it is now, right? It was still a nonprofit. I think there were maybe 50, 60 people total. And honestly most of the energy in the building was around RL. Like, this was the time of the Dota stuff, the robot hand, all that. And the language effort, I mean, calling it a team is generous. It was, like, a handful of people. So it was Alec Radford, who really drove that whole thing, Tim Salimans, Ilya, and then I was sort of the person who came in with the NLP background, right? Because I'd just finished the PhD, I knew what the tasks were, what the benchmarks were, how the NLP community actually evaluated things.

And the origin of that paper is kind of interesting because Alec had done this sentiment neuron work before, where he trained a character-level model on Amazon reviews and found that one unit in there was basically capturing sentiment on its own. So there was already this belief, at least from him, that if you just train a generative model on a lot of text, it'll pick up useful structure for free. And then the transformer paper came out in the middle of 2017, and the question was basically, okay, can we take this architecture, pretrain it on a bunch of unlabeled text, and then just fine-tune it on all these downstream tasks? Which sounds trivial now, right? Like, this is how everything works. But at that time in NLP the standard practice was you have your task, you design an architecture for that task. You have a separate model for entailment, a separate one for question answering, each with its own fancy attention mechanism. And so a lot of what I did was, like, take all these tasks and figure out how do you convert them into a format the same model can just consume. Like, how do you feed in a premise and a hypothesis, or a question and multiple choices, as one sequence with some delimiter tokens. And that's kind of the whole point of the paper, that you don't need task-specific architectures anymore.

And I remember it was a 12-layer transformer, like a hundred and something million parameters, trained on this BooksCorpus dataset, and to us that felt like a big run at the time. And the crazy thing was it just worked, right? Like, we got state of the art on nine of the twelve tasks we tried. And honestly, coming from NLP, I was a bit skeptical it would be that straightforward. But it was.

The funny part, though, is the reception at the time was pretty muted. Like, it came out as a blog post plus a PDF in June of 2018, and then a few months later BERT came out from Google and that's what everyone in NLP got excited about. GPT was sort of the thing that got a mention in the related work section. So if you had told me then that this was going to become the word that, like, everybody's grandparents now know, I would not have believed you. Nobody was thinking about ChatGPT. It was very much a research thing.

But I think there were two things I really took away from that year. One is just the value of simple ideas done well, right? There's nothing in that paper that's technically deep. It's take a good architecture, put a lot of data through it, and don't overthink the downstream part. And the second thing is it honestly shaped how I think about my role as an academic. Because I saw pretty early that compute and scale were going to matter a lot, and I knew I wasn't going to compete on that from a university. So a lot of what I do now, the benchmarks, the agents, the sort of looking a couple of steps ahead, is partly a consequence of that year. Like, okay, if I'm not going to be the one training the biggest model, where can I actually add value?
